Why Muscles Work in Pairs

Muscles can only pull — they cannot push. Because of this, every joint in the body is controlled by at least two muscles that work in opposite directions. When one muscle contracts and shortens to produce movement, the opposing muscle relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement. This arrangement is called an antagonistic muscle pair. OCR also requires knowledge of a third muscle role — the fixator — which stabilises a nearby joint while movement occurs at another.

Major Muscles of the Body

At the shoulder, the deltoid forms the rounded cap of the shoulder. It is the prime mover for abduction of the arm (lifting it out to the side) and also contributes to flexion and extension. The trapezius is the large, diamond-shaped muscle that runs from the base of the skull down to the middle of the back. It elevates the shoulders, pulls the scapula back and assists head movement. The latissimus dorsi (‘lats’) is the broad muscle of the lower and mid-back, responsible for extension and adduction of the arm at the shoulder — powerful in swimming backstroke and rowing movements. The pectorals (chest muscles) lie across the front of the thorax and act as prime movers in horizontal adduction, such as in the press-up or front crawl pull phase.

At the elbow, the biceps sits on the front of the upper arm. During elbow flexion (the upward phase of a bicep curl), the biceps is the agonist (prime mover), contracting and shortening to pull the forearm up. On the back of the upper arm sits the triceps. During elbow flexion, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing and lengthening to allow movement. The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the upward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist and the biceps becomes the antagonist. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder throughout the bicep curl, keeping the upper arm stable while the elbow moves.

The abdominals are the core muscles on the front of the trunk. They flex the spine, stabilise the pelvis during running and throwing, and are active in almost every sporting movement as a postural stabiliser and fixator.

At the hip and knee, two large muscle groups dominate. The quadriceps group (four muscles on the front of the thigh) is the prime mover for knee extension — straightening the knee. The hamstrings lie on the back of the thigh and are the prime mover for knee flexion (bending the knee). At the knee, the quadriceps and hamstrings form the classic antagonistic pair: quadriceps agonist during extension, hamstrings agonist during flexion. The gluteals are the large buttock muscles that drive hip extension — critical in sprinting and jumping.

At the ankle, the gastrocnemius runs from behind the knee down to the heel via the Achilles tendon. It is the prime mover for plantar flexion — pointing the toes down, as in sprinting push-off or jumping.

Key Fact

In the upward phase of a bicep curl: biceps = agonist (prime mover, contracts to flex the elbow), triceps = antagonist (relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement), deltoid = fixator (stabilises the shoulder joint so the upper arm stays still). In kicking (knee extension): quadriceps = agonist, hamstrings = antagonist.

Key Fact

The human body contains over 600 named muscles. Muscle fibres are packed with mitochondria — the organelles that produce ATP through aerobic respiration, supplying the energy needed for sustained muscular contraction during sport and exercise.

OCR explicitly requires three muscle roles — agonist, antagonist and fixator — while other boards only require two. Students who name only the agonist and antagonist will miss the fixator marks in OCR questions. A fixator is a muscle that holds a nearby body part still so that the prime mover can work efficiently. It does not produce the movement; it provides the stable base from which the movement occurs. In the bicep curl, the deltoid stabilises the shoulder joint throughout the exercise — without it, the shoulder would move and the elbow flexion would be inefficient. Always include the fixator and name the joint it stabilises.

A very common error in exams is to name a single muscle as ‘the agonist’ without specifying the joint, the direction of movement, or the antagonist and fixator. Mark schemes award marks for the complete picture: agonist named (1), antagonist named (1), fixator named and its role described (1), action described at the correct joint (1). Always frame answers as: “During elbow flexion, the biceps acts as the agonist (prime mover) while the triceps acts as the antagonist at the elbow joint. The deltoid acts as the fixator at the shoulder, stabilising the upper arm throughout the movement.”

What is a Motor Skill?

In physical education, a motor skill is a movement that has been deliberately learned and can be reproduced with accuracy and control. Unlike reflexes or instinctive reactions, motor skills are developed through practice. A novice footballer attempting a lofted pass for the first time is displaying very little skill; a county-level midfielder delivering a precise long ball under pressure has refined that movement through thousands of repetitions until it is consistent, efficient and goal-directed. The key idea is that motor skills are learned — they improve with practice and can be broken down, coached and refined.

Five Characteristics of Skilful Movement

OCR specifies five characteristics that distinguish a skilful movement from a clumsy or untrained one. When you watch an elite performer, all five are visible simultaneously.

Efficiency — a skilful movement uses only the muscles and energy required to complete the task. There is no wasted effort, no unnecessary tension and no redundant sub-movements. A seasoned marathon runner carries their arms low and relaxed; an elite swimmer pulls with a high elbow to maximise propulsion while minimising drag. Beginners waste energy through excess tension; skilled performers conserve it through economy of movement.

Pre-determined — a skilful movement has a clear intended outcome before it begins. The performer knows what they want to achieve and has a plan. A netball shooter stepping up for a penalty pass has already visualised the arc, the release point and the target before the ball leaves their hand. This intention guides the movement pattern from start to finish, rather than the performer discovering the outcome as they go.

Co-ordinated — different body parts work together in the correct sequence to produce the movement. In a javelin throw, the approach run, the crossover step, the hip drive, the shoulder rotation, the elbow extension and the wrist flick all combine in a precisely timed chain. If any link fires too early or too late, the sequence breaks down. Skilled performers produce these multi-limb co-ordinations fluently and automatically.

Fluent — the movement flows smoothly from one phase to the next without jerking, pausing or hesitation. Fluency is the visible sign that the performer has moved beyond the cognitive stage of learning (where each sub-routine is consciously executed) into the autonomous stage (where the movement runs automatically). A beginner swimming breaststroke will pause awkwardly between the pull and the kick; an experienced swimmer blends the phases seamlessly.

Aesthetic — a highly skilful movement is pleasing to watch. Not every sport rewards aesthetics formally (gymnastics and diving award marks for it; sprinting does not), but even in functional sports, observers recognise something visually satisfying about a perfectly struck golf drive, a clean double-leg takedown in wrestling, or a long-range curved shot curling into the top corner. Aesthetic quality is generally a by-product of the other four characteristics: a movement that is efficient, co-ordinated and fluent will tend to look graceful.

Key Fact

The five OCR characteristics of skilful movement are: efficiency (no wasted energy), pre-determined (clear intent before execution), co-ordinated (body parts linked in sequence), fluent (smooth, uninterrupted flow) and aesthetic (pleasing to observe). These apply to all motor skills, not just artistic sports.

The Two Skill Continua

OCR uses two continua to classify skills. A continuum is not a binary label but a spectrum — most skills fall between the two extremes, and the performer must justify the placement rather than simply attach a label. Both continua must be applied when classifying a skill for examination purposes.

Continuum 1: Simple to Complex (Difficulty)

The difficulty continuum runs from simple skills at one end to complex skills at the other. A simple skill demands very little from the performer in terms of decision-making, number of movements to co-ordinate simultaneously, or perceptual processing. Walking in a straight line, performing a standing jump, or rolling a ball along a flat surface are all towards the simple end.

A complex skill, at the other end, involves many sub-routines that must be co-ordinated simultaneously, a wide range of possible responses, and heavy demands on attention. A tennis serve — which requires the ball toss, stance, backswing, contact point and follow-through all to be synchronised — sits towards the complex end. A basketball lay-up sits between the two: it follows a set pattern (making it less complex) but requires simultaneous co-ordination of running, jumping and release angle (making it more demanding than a simple catch). The difficulty continuum is defined by how many decisions and sub-routines the skill involves, not by whether the environment is changing.

Continuum 2: Open to Closed (Environmental)

The environmental continuum describes how predictable the environment is while the skill is being performed. This is one of the most commonly confused continua in GCSE PE — open and closed refer to the environment, not to whether the skill is difficult. An open skill takes place in an unstable environment. A football pass under pressure from a defender is an open skill because the positions of teammates, defenders and the ball change from moment to moment, and the performer must adapt their movement continuously.

In contrast, a closed skill takes place in a stable, predictable environment. A gymnast performing a floor routine executes each element in the same unchanging space; a swimmer diving from the block always enters the same lane. Because the environment is fixed, the movement pattern can be pre-planned and repeated identically each time. The open-to-closed continuum is about environmental predictability, nothing else.

Many students write that a skill is “open because it is difficult” or “closed because it is simple” — this confuses the two continua and will lose marks. A highly complex gymnastics floor routine is a closed skill (environment is predictable and controlled) but sits at the complex end of the difficulty continuum. A simple one-touch pass in football is an open skill (defenders and teammates move unpredictably) but may be a straightforward movement in terms of co-ordination demands. Always base your open/closed answer on whether the environment is changing and unpredictable (open) or stable and predictable (closed). OCR only uses two continua — keep them clearly separate in your answers.

Key Fact

OCR uses only two skill continua: (1) Simple — Complex (difficulty): how many decisions, sub-routines and attentional demands the skill involves. (2) Open — Closed (environmental): how predictable and stable the environment is. Every skill classification answer should address both continua with justification. Most skills sit between the extremes, not at either end.

Worked Example: Classifying a Rugby Lineout Throw

A hooker throwing into a lineout can be placed on both continua. On the simple — complex continuum, the lineout throw sits towards the complex end: the hooker must co-ordinate the grip, run-up, elbow extension and wrist release while simultaneously reading where the jumpers are and which code the team has called. Multiple sub-routines and a range of decision-making demands push it away from the simple end. On the open — closed continuum, it sits towards the open end during match play: opposing players may disrupt the lineout, jumpers' positions change based on opposition movement, and the throw must adapt to a dynamic situation. However, during a training drill with no opposition, the same throw would shift towards the closed end — the environment is now predictable and the movement can be pre-planned.

On any skill classification question, simply writing “it is an open skill” earns no marks. Examiners require the justification: why is the skill open or complex? The justification must reference the correct definition — e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable; the positions of defenders and teammates change continuously so the performer must adapt”. The definition-based justification is what earns the mark, not the label. When placing a skill on the continuum, avoid placing it exactly at one extreme unless you can justify why it could not move any further in either direction — most realistic sport skills sit somewhere between the two poles.

Why Choose the Right Training Method?

Not all training is created equal. A marathon runner who only does heavy weight training will not improve her aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power he needs off the blocks. Training must be specific to the demands of the sport — this is the principle of specificity in action. Choosing the correct training method is therefore the first and most important decision a coach or athlete makes when designing a programme. OCR identifies seven training methods you need to know: continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a steady pace for a minimum of 20 minutes without any rest breaks. Activities such as running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all commonly used. Because the intensity remains constant and the body has a continuous oxygen supply, continuous training primarily develops cardiovascular endurance. It is well suited to distance runners, rowers and cyclists.

The main advantage is that it is simple, low-cost and easy to monitor — a runner simply keeps going at a steady pace within their aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). A disadvantage is that it can become repetitive and may not replicate the varied demands of team sports, which involve bursts of speed interspersed with periods of lower intensity.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training takes its name from the Swedish for “speed play.” Unlike standard continuous training, fartlek deliberately mixes periods of higher intensity effort with periods of slower recovery running, all without stopping. A footballer might jog steadily for two minutes, then sprint for 30 seconds, then stride at half-pace for a minute, then repeat. Because the performer decides when to change pace, it replicates the unpredictable demands of many team sports.

Key Fact

Fartlek means “speed play” in Swedish. It varies speed and terrain continuously, making it ideal for team-sport athletes whose games combine aerobic and anaerobic demands — such as footballers, rugby players and hockey players.

Interval Training

Interval training uses a planned work:rest ratio — a set period of hard effort followed by a set period of rest or low-intensity recovery. The athlete repeats this pattern for a fixed number of sets. For example, a 400 m track athlete might run 200 m at race pace, rest for 90 seconds, and repeat six times. By controlling the work:rest ratio, the coach can target either aerobic or anaerobic systems: longer work periods with short rests challenge the aerobic system, while very short, maximal sprints with longer rests target the anaerobic system.

Many students assume interval training is always anaerobic because of the repeated high-intensity efforts. In fact, the energy system targeted depends entirely on the work:rest ratio and intensity. A 3-minute effort at 65% maximum heart rate, with 1 minute of walking recovery, repeated five times, is aerobic interval training. Anaerobic interval training requires efforts above 80% of maximum heart rate with longer recovery periods. Always identify the intensity and duration to justify which energy system is being stressed — this is exactly the justification the mark scheme looks for.

HIIT

HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training) is a specific form of interval training where the work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity — typically above 80% of maximum heart rate, within the anaerobic training zone — and rest periods are short. A typical HIIT session might involve 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times. HIIT is time-efficient and produces improvements in both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, making it popular with athletes who are pressed for time.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, performing a specific exercise at each one before moving on to the next. A coach designing a circuit must consider: the space and equipment available, the number of stations, the work:rest ratio at each station, and the type of exercise at each station. The beauty of circuit training is its flexibility — by changing the exercises, the number of stations, the time at each station and the rest periods, the same circuit format can be adapted to develop cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength or power.

For example, a muscular endurance circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, tricep dips and step-ups, each performed for 45 seconds with 15 seconds to move to the next station. To make the same circuit develop strength instead, the coach would add resistance (using dumbbells or weighted vests), reduce the repetitions per station and increase the rest periods.

Weight Training

Weight training uses free weights, machines or bodyweight exercises with added resistance to develop muscular strength, power or muscular endurance. The fitness aim determines the weight and repetitions used. For strength and power, athletes use a high weight (above 70% of one rep max) and a low number of repetitions — approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, athletes use a lower weight (below 70% of one rep max) with a high number of repetitions — approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

Safe practice is non-negotiable: correct lifting technique prevents injury, appropriate weight selection avoids overloading, and a spotter should be present when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press or squat. The back should remain straight during deadlifts and squats to protect the lumbar vertebrae.

Key Fact

Strength/power training: above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps. Muscular endurance training: below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps. The fitness aim determines the weight and rep range.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training develops explosive power. The physiological basis is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle first undergoes a rapid lengthening phase as the athlete lands or prepares, storing elastic energy in the muscle and tendon; this is immediately followed by a powerful shortening contraction as the athlete jumps, bounds or throws. The faster the transition between these two phases, the greater the power output. Exercises include bounding, depth jumping, box jumps and medicine-ball throws. Plyometrics is well suited to sprinters, high jumpers, basketball players and volleyball players — any athlete who needs explosive leg or upper-body power.

Consider a county-level basketball player with a 10-week pre-season. Her coach wants to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular power and agility. An appropriate programme might combine: (1) fartlek training twice a week to mirror the stop-start aerobic and anaerobic demands of a basketball game; (2) plyometric training twice a week (depth jumps and bounding) to improve explosive jumping power for rebounds and lay-ups; (3) HIIT sessions to raise anaerobic threshold and improve the player’s ability to sustain high-intensity efforts late in the fourth quarter. Continuous training alone would be insufficient because it would not develop the anaerobic power the sport demands.

The Mental Side of Sport

Physical fitness and technical skill are not enough to guarantee peak performance. Elite athletes consistently report that the mental dimension of their preparation is as important as their physical training. Missing a penalty, misjudging a serve at a crucial moment, or freezing under pressure before a major competition — these experiences are not failures of technique alone. They reflect psychological factors that can be trained and managed. OCR identifies four mental preparation techniques that performers use to optimise their psychological readiness: imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Each technique addresses a different aspect of the performer’s mental state, and together they form a practical toolkit for performance preparation.

Imagery

Imagery is the deliberate creation of vivid mental pictures associated with sport. Unlike simply “thinking about” a sport, effective imagery engages multiple senses — the sound of the crowd, the texture of the ball, the sensation of the playing surface underfoot, the feeling of muscles working at full effort. A long-jumper preparing to compete might use imagery to experience, in vivid detail, the feeling of the approach run, the plant foot striking the board, the explosive drive of the hips and the moment of landing. A basketball player might image the sound of the ball swishing through the net.

Imagery works because the brain’s response to a vividly imagined experience shares many of the same neural pathways as the actual experience. Detailed, multi-sensory imaging creates a mental state of readiness that bridges the gap between preparation and competition. Imagery can also be used to manage nerves — a performer who has repeatedly imaged calm, controlled execution in a high-pressure moment is less likely to feel the situation as novel or overwhelming when it arrives. Adam Peaty has described using detailed imagery before major championship heats, imprinting a sense of familiarity onto what would otherwise feel like unique, high-stakes moments.

Mental Rehearsal

Mental rehearsal is the internal simulation of a complete performance or skill sequence, carried out in the mind before physical execution. Where imagery is primarily about creating a sensory experience, mental rehearsal has a more structured, procedural focus: the performer runs through the exact sequence of movements they intend to execute, in correct order, as if previewing the performance from inside their own body.

A diver performing a new list of dives at a national competition would use mental rehearsal to run through each dive in the correct sequence — approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck position, entry — several times before mounting the board. Research shows that mentally rehearsed movements activate many of the same motor pathways as physically performed movements, effectively providing “practice” that reinforces the movement programme without physical effort or risk. Mental rehearsal is most effective when performed in real time (not rushed), in the first person (from the performer’s own perspective), and always picturing successful execution rather than errors.

Key Fact

Imagery creates a vivid multi-sensory experience of sport, engaging feelings, sounds and visual detail — it prepares the mind for the competitive environment. Mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the skill sequence itself, rehearsing the exact movement programme before physical execution. Both techniques are used in the period before competition. Both picture success, never failure.

Selective Attention

Selective attention is the skill of directing focus towards the information that matters and filtering out everything else. Competition environments are full of potential distractions: crowd noise, opponents’ behaviour, negative internal thoughts, environmental conditions. A performer who has not trained their attention will find that these distractions invade their focus at precisely the moments when concentration is most critical.

Training selective attention means deliberately practising the ability to lock onto task-relevant cues — the flight of the ball, the position of a defender, the feel of the racket at contact — while choosing to ignore everything else. A tennis player preparing to receive a serve must direct all attention to the server’s ball toss and racket path, blocking out crowd noise, score awareness and anxiety about the point. A sprinter in the blocks must focus on the starting gun and their own movement activation, filtering out lane-side distractions and the presence of rivals. Dina Asher-Smith has spoken about developing a “tunnel vision” process in the call room before major finals, systematically narrowing attention to her own race plan.

Selective attention is developed through repeated practice, cueing routines (where the performer identifies specific cues to focus on) and mental preparation before competition. It is closely linked to both imagery and positive thinking — a performer who has imaged the task clearly and has a positive mental script is better able to focus on task-relevant cues because there is less cognitive space for distractions to fill.

Positive Thinking

Positive thinking involves consciously replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared, constructive thoughts. In sport, negative thinking is extremely common: “I always miss these”, “I’ve never done well in this arena”, “everyone is watching me”. Left unchallenged, negative thoughts reduce confidence, tighten muscles, narrow attention in unhelpful ways and can trigger the self-fulfilling prophecy of poor performance. Positive thinking is the deliberate psychological counterattack.

The technique works by having the performer prepare a set of positive, task-focused mental statements in advance of competition. These statements are not empty slogans but specific, believable reminders that redirect attention towards what the performer can do: “I have trained this kick hundreds of times”, “I trust my technique”, “smooth contact, follow through”. When negative thoughts arise — and in high-pressure moments they will — the performer activates their prepared positive script, interrupting the negative loop and redirecting focus to the execution cues.

Positive thinking does not require ignoring difficulty or pretending a situation is not pressured. It is realistic self-support: acknowledging the importance of the moment while maintaining belief in preparation. A rugby goal kicker who thinks “this kick matters AND I have the skill to execute it” is using positive thinking effectively. A kicker who tells themselves “this is fine, I never miss” when their recent form has been poor is not — that is denial, which collapses under real pressure.

Elite athletes rarely use just one mental preparation technique in isolation. Before a major competition, a gymnast might use mental rehearsal (running through the floor routine in sequence), imagery (experiencing the feel and sound of the hall and the sensation of the tumble run), selective attention (narrowing focus to the floor and the music, filtering out the score and the audience), and positive thinking (“I have trained this routine for six months — my body knows what to do”). Together, the four techniques create a psychological state of readiness in which the performer is fully focused on successful execution. In an exam, you may be asked to explain how one specific technique works or to evaluate the relative usefulness of the four techniques — make sure you can describe the mechanism of each separately before discussing how they combine.

Key Fact

Four OCR mental preparation techniques: (1) Imagery — vivid multi-sensory mental pictures that prepare the mind for competition. (2) Mental rehearsal — a structured run-through of the skill sequence in the mind before physical execution. (3) Selective attention — focusing on task-relevant cues while filtering out distractions. (4) Positive thinking — replacing negative internal dialogue with prepared positive scripts to maintain confidence.

OCR’s sports psychology unit covers the four techniques above and no more in this section. The following topics appear on other examination boards but are NOT assessed by OCR and should not appear in your answers: arousal and the inverted-U theory; information processing models; personality types; aggression types; motivation types; contract to compete. If a question asks you about mental preparation in sport, restrict your answer to imagery, mental rehearsal, selective attention and positive thinking. Adding content from outside the OCR specification will not gain marks and may suggest to the examiner that you are confused about the scope of the course.
